/2016/01/how-to-make-hood-for-cloak-or-c.title: How to Make a Hood for a Cloak or Cape (No Pattern)
/2016/01/how-to-make-hood-for-cloak-or-c.description: Make a hood for a cloak or cape without a pattern: take three easy measurements, draw the hood shape on folded fabric, then sew it. Photos for each step.
/2016/01/how-to-make-hood-for-cloak-or-c.append:
Hood Size Tips Before You Cut

Updated October 2026: extra sizing tips and answers to common questions, added by the Just Halloween Crafts team.

The three measurements above work for children and adults alike, but hoods are forgiving, so it is worth spending two minutes on a test before cutting into good fabric.

  • Make a paper mock-up first. Draw the hood shape on newspaper or wrapping paper, tape the back curve together and try it on. If the front edge sits on the forehead and the paper does not pull at the neck, the size is right.
  • Go bigger rather than smaller. A roomy hood drapes in soft folds and looks more dramatic. A tight hood pulls the cloak backwards and slides off the head.
  • Allow for hair and hats. Add a little extra to Measurement B if the wearer has a bun, long thick hair, or will wear a hat or horns underneath.
  • Thick fabric needs more ease. Velvet, fleece and heavy curtain fabric take up more room in the seams than cotton, so add an extra half inch (1 cm) or so to each measurement.

How do I make a pointed hood?

Extend the curved back line upwards into a gentle point instead of rounding it off at the top corner. The longer the point, the more it will flop over, which suits elf, wizard and witch costumes. Try the shape in paper first, because a point that looks small on the table can look very long once it is worn.

Can I line the hood?

Yes. Cut the hood twice, once in your main fabric and once in a lining such as satin or cotton. Sew the back seam of each piece separately, then place them right sides together and stitch along the front opening. Turn the hood right side out, press the front edge and treat both layers as one when you attach it to the cape. A contrast lining, such as red inside a black hood, is an easy way to make a simple costume look special.

Can I make a hood without a sewing machine?

You can. Hand sew the back seam with a small backstitch, which is strong enough for a costume. If you use fleece or felt, the edges will not fray, so you can skip hemming the front opening altogether.

Not sure which fabric to buy? Our guide to the best fabric for a cloak or cape compares the most popular choices. The same hood also works on a DIY wizard robe or a no-sew cloak. When the hood is ready, follow the steps to sew the hood onto your cape.

How do you make a hood for a cape you already have?

Measure the cape's neckline along the curve first: the bottom edge of the finished hood must match it, minus a small gap at the front. Then draw the hood shape from your head measurements, test it in paper and sew it on. For a cape and hood made together from scratch, follow our guide on how to make a hooded cloak.
/2016/01/how-to-make-hood-for-cloak-or-c.prepend:
How to Sew a Hood: The Short Answer

To make a hood for a cloak, cape or any costume, take three head measurements, draw a hood shape on folded fabric, sew the curved back seam, hem the face opening and stitch the bottom edge to the cape's neckline. You don't need a pattern, and the same method works for fleece, cotton, velvet or an old curtain.

  1. Measure from the top of the head to the shoulder, around the face from neck to neck, and from the forehead to the back of the head.
  2. Fold your fabric in half and draw the hood shape from those measurements, adding a seam allowance on every edge. Test it in paper first if you're unsure.
  3. Cut through both layers, sew the curved back seam and turn the hood right side out.
  4. Hem the front opening (fleece and felt can be left raw) and sew the hood to the cape's neckline.

The full photo tutorial with every measurement explained is below.

/2015/07/how-to-sew-hood-onto-cape.title: How to Sew a Hood onto a Cape or Cloak, Step by Step
/2015/07/how-to-sew-hood-onto-cape.description: How to sew a hood onto a cape or cloak: match the center back, pin and ease the neckline, stitch, clip the curve and finish the seam so the hood sits well.
/2015/07/how-to-sew-hood-onto-cape.append:
Extra Tips for Attaching a Hood Neatly

Updated October 2026: extra tips and fixes added by the Just Halloween Crafts team.

The three steps above are all you need for a quick costume. If you want the join to look a little more polished, or the hood is not sitting quite right, these extra steps help.

  1. Compare the two edges before pinning. Measure the bottom edge of the hood and the neckline of the cape. A difference of an inch (2 to 3 cm) is easy to ease in. If the hood is much wider, take a slightly deeper seam at the center back of the hood or fold two small pleats on either side of the center point.
  2. Stay-stitch the cape neckline. Sew a line of straight stitching about 3/8 inch (1 cm) inside the curved neck edge before you pin. Curved edges stretch when they are handled, and this stops the neckline from growing out of shape.
  3. Tack it first. Run a line of long, loose hand stitches along the pinned seam and try the cloak on. It is much easier to adjust a tacked seam than to unpick machine stitching.
  4. Clip the curve. After sewing, snip into the seam allowance every inch or so, stopping just short of the stitching. This lets the curved seam lie flat instead of puckering.
  5. Finish the raw edges. Zigzag or overlock the two layers of seam allowance together, press them towards the cape, then topstitch close to the seam. Covering the seam with ribbon or bias binding, as mentioned above, also gives a tidy finish.
  6. Add a fastening. Sew ribbon ties, a large hook and eye or a decorative cloak clasp at the front corners of the neckline. For young children, choose a hook and eye or hook-and-loop tape rather than long ties around the neck.

Common Problems and Quick Fixes

  • The hood pulls backwards and tugs at the throat. The hood is too shallow from front to back. Make a new hood with a larger front-to-back measurement, or add a strip of fabric along the front edge.
  • The hood falls over the eyes. It is deeper than needed. Fold back a cuff along the front edge and stitch it in place, or take a tuck at the top of the back seam.
  • There are small puckers along the seam. The extra fabric was not spread evenly. Unpick just that section, redistribute the pins and sew it again.

Heavy fabrics such as curtain material, velvet and fleece drape well but are bulkier at the seams, so trim the seam allowance a little before finishing. For more help choosing material, see the best fabric for a cloak or cape.

Finish the Neckline: Add a Closure

Updated October 2026: closure, seam-finishing tips and FAQ added by the Just Halloween Crafts team.

Once the hood is on, the cloak needs a way to close at the front. Sew it just below the hood seam so the hood can fall back freely. Fabric ties are the quickest, a metal cloak clasp or frog closure gives a fantasy look, and a hook-and-loop tab is safest for children because it pulls apart if the cloak gets caught. Our guide on how to fasten a cloak or cape shows how to sew on each one.

Hood and Cape FAQ

Can I attach a hood to a cape without sewing?

Yes, if you use fleece. Fold a fleece rectangle into a hood, close the back with fringe knots, then thread one drawstring through slits in both the hood and the cape's neckline. Our no-sew cloak guide shows the method step by step.

Should I attach the hood before or after hemming the cape?

Attach the hood first, then hem the front edges and bottom. That way the front edges of the hood and cape can be hemmed in one line for a neater finish.

Making the cloak from scratch? See how to make a hood for a cloak, how to sew a cloak without a pattern and our best fabric for a cloak guide, or follow the complete hooded cloak tutorial that takes you through every step in order.
/2015/07/how-to-sew-hood-onto-cape.prepend: Quick answer: to attach a hood to a cape, find the middle of the hood's bottom edge and the middle of the cape's neckline, pin them together right sides facing, then pin outward to each front edge, easing or tucking any extra fabric. Sew along the pinned line with a straight stitch, and cover the seam with ribbon if you want a neat finish inside.

/2015/08/how-to-sew-cloak-without-patter.title: How to Sew a Cloak or Cape Without a Pattern
/2015/08/how-to-sew-cloak-without-patter.description: Sew a simple unlined cloak or cape without a pattern: take two measurements, cut one piece of fabric with a curved neck, then hem it. Hooded option included.
/2015/08/how-to-sew-cloak-without-patter.append:
Quick Answers Before You Buy Fabric

Updated October 2026: fabric and no-sew tips added by the Just Halloween Crafts team.

What if my fabric is not wide enough?

Most dressmaking fabric is sold in widths of about 44 to 60 inches (112 to 150 cm). An adult floor-length cloak can need a piece wider than that. The simplest fix is to cut two pieces and join them with a seam down the center back, where it will hardly show once the cloak is worn. Old curtains and bed sheets, like the fabric used here, are often wide enough to cut the whole cloak in one piece.

Which fabric is easiest for a first cloak?

Fleece is the friendliest choice: it does not fray, so the hems can be left raw, and it is warm for outdoor trick or treating. Cotton drill or poplin is easy to sew but does not drape as dramatically. Velvet and satin look wonderful but slip and shift, so they are better once you have made one cloak already. Our guide to the best fabric for a cloak or cape goes into more detail.

Can I make the cloak without sewing?

Yes, if you use fleece or felt. Cut the shape exactly as described above, leave the edges raw and finish the neckline by snipping pairs of small slits about an inch apart and threading a ribbon through them as a drawstring. Fabric glue can also hold a folded hem in place, although it is not as hard-wearing as stitching.

How long should a child's cloak be?

Stop at the ankle or just above it. A cloak that touches the floor looks great in photos but is easy to trip over on steps and doorways, especially in the dark on Halloween night.

Want a hood? Follow the tutorial on how to make a hood for a cloak and then how to sew the hood onto the cape.

How to Sew a Cloak With a Hood

To sew a cloak with a hood, make the cloak body first, then sew a separate two-piece hood and stitch it to the neckline before you hem the front edges. The cloak above is cut as one large piece, so the hood is the only extra part, and it adds roughly an hour to the project.

  1. Cut and finish the cloak body exactly as described above, but leave the neckline raw for now.
  2. Measure from the base of the neck, over the top of the head, to the other side of the neck, and from the forehead to the back of the neck. Add room for movement and seam allowances, then cut two matching hood pieces. Our tutorial on how to make a hood for a cloak shows the shape and the measurements step by step.
  3. Sew the two hood pieces together along the curved back seam and hem the front edge of the hood (the edge that frames the face).
  4. Pin the open bottom edge of the hood to the cloak neckline, right sides together, matching the back seam of the hood to the center back of the cloak. Ease the fabric so it sits evenly, then stitch. The step-by-step photos in how to sew a hood onto a cape show this part.
  5. Finish the neckline seam with a zigzag stitch, then add ties, a ribbon or a clasp at the throat.

Prefer to follow the whole hooded project in one place, from measuring to the final clasp? Our step-by-step guide on how to make a hooded cloak covers the body, the hood, joining them and a troubleshooting table.

How to Make a Cloak Without a Hood

A cloak without a hood is the same project with one step left out: cut the body, finish the edges and add a fastening at the neck. Because there is no hood to hold the neckline in shape, it helps to make the neck a little snugger than for a hooded cloak, or to fold the neck edge over to make a channel and thread a ribbon through it as a drawstring. A stand-up collar, cut as a long rectangle of stiff fabric and stitched to the neckline, gives a hoodless cloak a more dramatic look for vampires and wizards.

More Cloak and Cape FAQs

How do you make a cloak without a pattern?

Take two measurements, the length from shoulder to ankle and the loose neck size, then fold a rectangle of fabric in half and mark two quarter circles from the folded corner: a small one for the neck and a large one for the length. Cut through both layers and you have a half-circle cloak ready to hem.

Is a cloak the same as a cape?

The words are often used interchangeably for costumes. In general a cape is shorter and hangs from the shoulders, while a cloak is longer, fuller and often has a hood. The method on this page works for both: change measurement A to make it shorter or longer.

Can I make a cloak with a hood without sewing?

Yes, with fleece or felt, which do not fray. Cut the body and hood as usual, then join the hood to the neckline with fabric glue or iron-on hemming tape, overlapping the edges by about an inch. Let the glue cure fully before wearing, and expect a sewn seam to last longer.

How to Print and Use the Half Butterfly Template

Updated October 2026: printing and project tips added by the Just Halloween Crafts team.

  1. Open the full-size image and save it to your computer or phone before printing, so you print the large version rather than the smaller preview.
  2. Choose "fit to page" in your printer settings. The design fills a standard letter or A4 sheet. To make a smaller butterfly, set the print scale to 50 or 75 percent.
  3. Print on card if you can. Thin card or cardstock makes a sturdier template that you can trace around again and again.
  4. Make a full butterfly. Fold a sheet of card or paper in half. Line up the straight body edge of the template with the fold, trace around it and cut through both layers. When you open it out, you have a complete, symmetrical butterfly.

Halloween Ideas for the Butterfly Silhouette

  • Cut a swarm of black butterflies or moths from card and fix them to a wall or mirror with removable adhesive putty for a gothic display.
  • Tape black paper butterflies to a window so they show up as silhouettes when the room is lit at night.
  • Use the template to cut felt butterflies, as in this hanging felt butterfly decoration.
  • Trace it onto a painted pumpkin or a plain cushion cover as a guide for paint or fabric pens.

Ways to Use These Crow Silhouettes

Updated October 2026: project ideas and printing tips added by the Just Halloween Crafts team.

Crow shapes work best when they are cut from solid black card, because the outline is what makes them recognizable. A few ideas to get you started:

  • Window crows. Cut several birds in different sizes and tape them to the inside of a window. With the lights on after dark they look like a flock perched outside.
  • Mantel or shelf birds. Glue a cutout to a wooden skewer and push the skewer into a pot, a pumpkin or a block of florist's foam so the crow stands upright.
  • A flock on the wall. Arrange flying crows in a loose diagonal line across a wall or up a staircase, fixed with removable adhesive putty.
  • Pumpkin stencils. Tape a printed crow onto a pumpkin and trace or prick around the outline, then paint or carve the shape.
  • Cards and banners. Glue small crows onto folded card for party invitations, or add them to a homemade Halloween banner.

Printing Tips

Open each image at full size before printing so the edges stay crisp. If you want to save black ink, print the birds on plain paper as templates, then trace around them onto black card. To make a bigger crow, increase the scale in your printer settings or print the image across two sheets and tape them together.

For a ready-made project using these shapes, see the black crow craft cutouts tutorial, or browse more raven and crow crafts.

/2015/07/free-maleficent-horn-template-t.title: Free Maleficent Horns Template to Print and Cut
/2015/07/free-maleficent-horn-template-t.description: A free printable Maleficent horns template for a Halloween costume. Print it, trace it onto card or craft foam and make a horn mask or headband.
/2015/07/free-maleficent-horn-template-t.append:
How to Use the Maleficent Horn Template

Updated October 2026: step-by-step tips added by the Just Halloween Crafts team.

  1. Print at the right size. Print the template at 100 percent for a child. For an adult, increase the scale to around 120 to 130 percent and hold the paper horns against the wearer's head before cutting anything.
  2. Choose a material. Black craft foam (EVA foam) is light and easy to cut. Thin card is fine for a one-night costume. For a headpiece that will be worn again and again, layer two pieces of card or foam and glue them together.
  3. Trace and cut. Draw around the template with a white pencil or silver pen so the line shows up on black material, then cut slightly inside the line for a neat edge.
  4. Add the details. A few lines of black or dark grey paint across each horn suggest ridges. A little glitter or shimmer paint catches the light at a party.
  5. Attach the horns. Glue them to a hair band, or add elastic for a simple mask. The Maleficent horn headband tutorial shows a sturdier version step by step.

Keep the horns away from candles and lanterns, especially if you use foam or paper. For more ideas, see all Maleficent crafts and costume ideas or the full list of DIY costume accessories.

/2015/10/free-halloween-potion-bottle-la.description: Free printable Halloween potion bottle labels with an aged parchment look. Print, cut and stick them on jars and bottles for a spooky apothecary shelf.
/2015/10/free-halloween-potion-bottle-la.append:
Tips for Better Looking Potion Labels

Updated October 2026: printing and finishing tips added by the Just Halloween Crafts team.

  • Print on matte paper. Ordinary printer paper or matte photo paper suits the old parchment style better than glossy paper.
  • Age the edges. Rub the cut edges with a used tea bag or brush on a little cold coffee, then leave the labels to dry flat. Lightly tearing the edges instead of cutting them also makes the labels look older.
  • Stick them on smoothly. Brush a thin layer of PVA or school glue on the back of the label, press it onto a clean, dry bottle and smooth out any bubbles with a soft cloth. A coat of decoupage medium over the top protects the label from damp fingers.
  • Use a sticker sheet for speed. Printable sticker paper means no glue at all, which is handy when you are labelling a whole shelf of bottles.

Need bottles to put the labels on? Our step-by-step guide to making DIY potion bottles shows how to fill, cork and age them. You can also print the Princess Bride potion labels for a themed set.

Single Ring, Double Ring or Store-Bought Frame?

Updated October 2026: frame comparison, decorating guide link and FAQ added by the Just Halloween Crafts team.

A single hanger ring is enough for wrapped ribbon, yarn or tulle tied in bunches. A double ring, made by joining two circles of slightly different sizes as described above, gives you more to tie onto and holds fuller coverings such as fabric strips. Store-bought box frames, with three or four rings joined by cross bars, are best for very full deco mesh wreaths.

Next Step: Decorate Your Wire Wreath Frame

Once your frame is ready, cover the wire completely, then add your Halloween details. Our step-by-step guide on how to decorate a wire wreath frame for Halloween covers four coverings (deco mesh, tulle, wrapped ribbon and fabric strips) and how to attach spiders, bats and a bow so they stay put.

Wire Wreath Frame FAQ

What gauge wire is best for a wreath frame?

A standard wire coat hanger is stiff enough for most door wreaths. If you buy wire, remember that a lower gauge number means thicker, stiffer wire, so choose a low gauge for a frame and keep thin, high-gauge floral wire for attaching decorations.

How do I stop a wire wreath frame from rusting?

Wrap the frame completely in ribbon, tape or fabric before you decorate it, and hang outdoor wreaths under a porch roof or on a door that's sheltered from rain. Bring the wreath indoors after the season to dry and store.

Can I make a wreath frame without wire?

Yes. A ring cut from sturdy cardboard makes a good frame for indoor wreaths. See our cardboard wreath form tutorial. Cardboard isn't suitable outdoors, because it softens when it gets damp.

/2016/07/how-to-make-paper-spider-webs-k.description: How to make a paper spider web: fold a paper circle, cut narrow notches along the edges and open it out. Easy Halloween craft for kids aged 3 and up.
/2016/07/how-to-make-paper-spider-webs-k.prepend: Quick answer: to make a paper spider web, cut out a large paper circle, fold it in half three or four times into a narrow wedge, cut small notches in from both long sides (alternating, like a paper snowflake) and unfold it. Draw rings with a marker to join the spokes and finish the web look.
/2016/07/how-to-make-paper-spider-webs-k.append:
Paper Spider Web Steps at a Glance

Updated October 2026: summary, troubleshooting and FAQ added by the Just Halloween Crafts team.

  1. Draw around a dinner plate on colored paper and cut out the circle. A bigger circle is easier for small hands to fold and cut.
  2. Fold the circle in half, then in half again, then once or twice more until you have a narrow wedge.
  3. Cut short, narrow notches in from both long edges of the wedge, alternating sides and leaving uncut paper between them so the web holds together.
  4. Snip a tiny piece off the point if you want a hole in the middle.
  5. Unfold carefully, press flat under a book and draw curved lines between the folds to make the rings of the web.

Troubleshooting Paper Spider Webs

  • The web fell apart when opened. The notches met in the middle. Leave a strip of uncut paper of about a quarter of an inch (half a centimetre) between cuts from opposite sides.
  • It is too hard to cut. There are too many layers. Use printer paper rather than card, or fold one time fewer.
  • It does not look like a web. Cut thinner notches closer together, and add rings with a marker, white crayon on black paper, or glued yarn.

Ways to Use Your Webs

Tape them to windows, hang several at different heights with thread, or glue one onto a card. Black paper webs look striking on an orange door, and white webs show up well on dark walls. Add a pom pom spider or use the webs as the background for a spider web banner. For more cut-and-make projects, browse our free printable Halloween crafts, from crow silhouettes to banner letters.

Paper Spider Web FAQ

What age is this paper spider web craft for?

Children who can use child-safe scissors, usually from about age 3 or 4, can make a simple web with help folding. Five and six year olds can often do the whole thing themselves. Younger children can decorate a web an adult has cut out, adding rings with crayons and a sticker spider.

What paper works best?

Ordinary printer paper or thin origami paper folds and cuts most easily. Construction paper gives brighter colors but becomes thick after several folds, so fold it one time fewer. Metallic or patterned paper makes webs that stand out in a window.

How do you make a paper spider web without a circle?

Start with a square instead: fold it diagonally into a triangle three times, trim the open edge into a curve and then cut notches as usual. Unfolded, it makes a round web just like the circle method.

/2018/12/perler-bead-spider-web.title: Perler Bead Spider Web: Easy Halloween Pattern Steps
/2018/12/perler-bead-spider-web.description: Make a Perler bead spider web on a hexagon pegboard: lay three spokes, add two rings of beads, then iron. Hang it as decor or use it as a cupcake topper.
/2018/12/perler-bead-spider-web.append:
Perler Bead Spider Web Pattern in 4 Steps

Updated October 2026: summary, ironing tips and FAQ added by the Just Halloween Crafts team.

A Perler bead spider web is three straight lines of beads crossing in the middle of a hexagon pegboard, with two rings of beads woven between them, fused with an iron. Here is the whole pattern in brief:

  1. Turn a hexagon pegboard so one point faces you, then lay a straight line of beads from the bottom point to the top point.
  2. Add two diagonal lines corner to corner so you have six spokes meeting in the center.
  3. Fill in two rings of beads between the spokes, one near the middle and one near the edge.
  4. Cover with ironing paper and iron, then flip and iron the back lightly so the web is strong enough to hang.

Ironing Tips for a Strong Web

Spider webs have lots of thin lines, so they are more fragile than solid designs. Iron with gentle, circular movements on a medium setting until the beads just start to merge, then lift the paper and check. A web that is fused a little more than usual on both sides is less likely to snap at the spokes. Press it under a heavy book while it cools to keep it flat. Ironing is a job for an adult or an older child with supervision.

Ideas for Your Finished Webs

  • Window and tree ornaments: thread a loop of fishing line or ribbon through one of the outer beads.
  • Cupcake toppers: wash the fused webs and press one into the frosting just before serving, or make toppers you can actually eat with our edible Halloween crafts and spider cupcake ideas.
  • Magnets and keychains: glue a small magnet to the back or add a key ring through an outer bead.

For more patterns, see our Halloween Perler bead patterns, and for paper projects you can print at home, our roundup of free printable Halloween crafts.

Perler Bead Spider Web FAQ

Can I make a spider web on a square pegboard?

Yes, but it is harder to keep the spokes even. Use the diagonal lines of the square board for four of the spokes and the middle row and column for the rest. A hexagon board gives the neatest six-sided web with the least counting.

How many beads does a spider web take?

It depends on the size of the board and how many rings you add. Count as you lay the spokes and fill a small cup with a few extra beads of the same color before you start, so you are not hunting for matching beads halfway through.

Are Perler beads safe for young children?

Standard fuse beads are small parts and are not suitable for children under three. Larger beads made for younger children are available, and a grown-up should always do or supervise the ironing.

/2017/11/hobbit-feet-cookies.title: Feet Cookies: How to Make Hairy Hobbit Feet Cookies
/2017/11/hobbit-feet-cookies.description: How to make feet cookies: cut vanilla sugar cookies with a foot cutter, pipe chocolate toenails and add grated chocolate hair. A fun Halloween bake.
/2017/11/hobbit-feet-cookies.append:
Feet Cookies Without a Foot Cutter

Updated October 2026: tips and FAQ added by the Just Halloween Crafts team.

No foot-shaped cutter? Cut an oval with a round cutter or a glass and gently pinch one end narrower to make a heel. Press five small balls of dough along the wide end for toes before baking. Another option is to draw a foot on baking paper, cut it out and use it as a template, cutting around it with a small sharp knife.

Decorating Tips for Hairy Feet

  • Let the cookies cool completely before decorating, or the chocolate will melt into them.
  • Pipe the toenails first and let them set, then add the hair, so the nails stay neat.
  • Chocolate sprinkles, toasted coconut or chocolate cereal flakes all work as hair if you do not want to grate chocolate.
  • Use white chocolate tinted with a little cocoa for lighter hair, or make a mix of shades for a whole family of feet.

Making Them Ahead

The cookie dough can be made a day ahead and kept wrapped in the fridge. Baked, undecorated cookies keep in an airtight tin for a few days. Decorate on the day of the party for the neatest finish, and store the decorated cookies in a single layer so the hair does not get squashed.

Looking for more party food? Try our edible Halloween crafts kids can make, zombie cookies or these savory Halloween snacks for guests without a sweet tooth.

Feet Cookies FAQ

What are feet cookies?

Feet cookies are sugar cookies cut into the shape of a foot and decorated with toes, toenails or, for Hobbit feet, chocolate hair. They are a popular novelty bake for Halloween, fantasy-themed parties and birthdays.

Can I use ready-made cookie dough?

Yes. Chill shop-bought sugar cookie dough well before rolling so the feet keep their shape in the oven, and follow the baking time on the pack. Decorate exactly as described above.

How do I stop the cookies spreading?

Chill the cut-out feet on the baking tray for about 10 minutes before baking, do not over-soften the butter, and roll the dough evenly so the toes do not burn before the middle is cooked.

/2015/06/savory-halloween-appetizers-and.title: Savory Halloween Snacks and Appetizers: Easy Party Ideas
/2015/06/savory-halloween-appetizers-and.description: Easy savory Halloween snacks and appetizers: carved orange dip bowls, eyeball tomatoes, stuffed dates, mummy sausages and more spooky party food ideas.
/2015/06/savory-halloween-appetizers-and.prepend: Quick answer: the easiest savory Halloween snacks are everyday party food with a spooky name and presentation: dips served in carved oranges or mini pumpkins, stuffed cherry tomato "eyeballs", stuffed dates in a coffin box, coleslaw with raisin "flies", breadstick "witch fingers" and pastry-wrapped mummy sausages.
/2015/06/savory-halloween-appetizers-and.append:
More Savory Halloween Snack Ideas

Updated October 2026: extra ideas, make-ahead tips and FAQ added by the Just Halloween Crafts team.

These ideas use simple ingredients and lean on presentation rather than complicated recipes, in the same spirit as the snacks above.

Mummy sausages

Cut ready-rolled puff pastry into thin strips and wrap them around cocktail sausages or hot dogs, leaving a gap near one end for the face. Bake until the pastry is golden and the sausages are hot through, then add two dots of mustard or ketchup for eyes.

Cheese and cracker spiders

Sandwich a little cream cheese between two round crackers, push four short pretzel sticks into each side for legs and add two dots of cream cheese with a peppercorn or a sliver of olive for eyes.

Black olive spiders

Halve pitted black olives. Use one half as the body and slice the other half into thin strips for legs. They look great scattered over a pizza, a bowl of hummus or a plate of deviled eggs.

Spider web dip

Spread a layer of hummus, refried beans or guacamole on a plate. Pipe circles of sour cream on top, then drag a toothpick from the center outwards to make a web. Serve with tortilla chips and vegetable sticks.

Pizza faces

Top English muffin halves or mini pizza bases with tomato sauce, then make jack-o'-lantern faces with pepper triangles, or mummy faces with strips of mozzarella and olive-slice eyes. Children can assemble their own before an adult bakes them.

Make-Ahead Tips for a Halloween Party

  • Make dips the day before and keep them covered in the fridge. Carve the orange or pumpkin bowls on the day.
  • Stuffed tomatoes and dates can be prepared a few hours ahead and chilled until guests arrive.
  • Assemble pastry mummies in the morning, keep them chilled on the tray and bake just before serving.
  • Label every dish with a spooky name and a small card listing common allergens such as nuts, dairy, gluten and egg.

For something kids can make themselves, see our edible Halloween crafts. For serving ideas, see our Halloween dip bowls and mini pumpkin dip bowl.

Savory Halloween Snacks FAQ

What are good savory Halloween snacks for a party?

Choose finger food that guests can eat standing up: stuffed tomatoes, mummy sausages, cracker spiders, cheese-stuffed dates and dips with breadsticks or vegetable sticks. Give each one a spooky name and serve it in a themed bowl or box for the Halloween effect.

How can I make savory food look scary?

Use color and shape: olives for spiders and eyes, red sauces for "blood", pastry strips for mummy bandages and green dips for "slime". Serving in carved oranges, mini pumpkins or a coffin-shaped box adds atmosphere with little extra work.

What savory snacks can kids help make?

Cracker spiders, pizza faces and olive spiders are easy for children to assemble. Leave cutting, coring and anything involving the oven to an adult, and check for food allergies before the party.

/2015/06/pumpkin-trick-or-treat-bag-felt.title: Felt Pumpkin Trick or Treat Bag: Free Sewing Pattern
/2015/06/pumpkin-trick-or-treat-bag-felt.description: Sew a felt pumpkin trick or treat bag with this free pattern: three overlapping circles, a leaf and ribbon handles. Size guide, sewing tips and FAQ.
/2015/06/pumpkin-trick-or-treat-bag-felt.prepend: Quick answer: to sew a felt pumpkin trick or treat bag, cut three equal circles of orange felt, overlap two side by side and lay the third on top in the middle, then stitch them together. Trace that shape onto more felt for the back, add a green leaf and ribbon stem, sew the front to the back around the bottom and sides, and finish with ribbon handles.
/2015/06/pumpkin-trick-or-treat-bag-felt.append:
Pumpkin Bag Size Guide

Updated October 2026: size guide, sewing tips and FAQ added by the Just Halloween Crafts team.

The circle you trace decides the size of the bag. As the steps above explain, the finished bag is about one and a half circles wide and about one circle tall, not counting the handles. Measure your plate or bowl across the middle and use this as a guide:

Circle traced aroundTypical circle sizeFinished bag (approx.)Good for
Mug3 to 4 in (8 to 10 cm)5 to 6 in wideParty favor bags
Cereal bowl6 in (15 cm)About 9 in wideToddlers and preschoolers
Salad plate7 to 8 in (18 to 20 cm)About 11 in wideChildren up to about eight
Dinner plate10 to 11 in (25 to 28 cm)About 15 in wideOlder children and big candy hauls

Craft felt is often sold in 9 by 12 inch sheets, so circles larger than about 8 inches need felt cut from a roll or bolt.

Tips for a Stronger Pumpkin Bag

  • Use a machine or backstitch: a sewing machine makes the strongest seams. By hand, use a backstitch rather than a running stitch for the seams that carry the weight.
  • Reinforce the handles: sew each handle end with a small square of stitches with an X through it, and place the handles inside the top edge so the stitches aren't pulled outward.
  • Choose thicker felt: thin acrylic craft felt stretches when the bag is full. Wool-blend or stiffened felt holds its shape better.
  • Add a lining: cut the same shape from cotton fabric, sew it into a pocket and slip it inside the bag before you stitch the top edge. It stops the felt from stretching and keeps wrappers from catching.
  • No-sew option: for a decoration or a light party favor bag, glue the layers with fabric glue and let it dry fully. Glued bags are not strong enough for a full night of trick-or-treating.

For trick-or-treating after dark, add a strip of reflective tape to the back of the bag. Want more felt projects? Try our felt Halloween finger puppets, see more treat and favor bags, or make a matching costume with our no-sew cloak guide.

Pumpkin Trick or Treat Bag FAQ

What felt is best for a trick or treat bag?

Thicker felt makes the best trick or treat bag because it holds its shape and doesn't stretch when the bag is full. Wool-blend or stiffened craft felt works well. Thin acrylic felt is fine for small favor bags, or you can add a cotton lining to make it stronger.

Can I sew this pumpkin bag by hand?

Yes. Every step can be sewn by hand with a needle and thread. Use a backstitch for the side seams and handles, because it is much stronger than a running stitch, and sew the leaf and trim with a simple running or blanket stitch.

How do I make the pumpkin bag bigger?

Trace a bigger circle. The finished bag is roughly one and a half circles wide and one circle tall, so a dinner plate makes a bag big enough for older children. Larger circles need felt from a roll, since standard craft sheets are too small.

/2017/09/pumpkin-fairy-house.title: Pumpkin Fairy House Carving: Step-by-Step with Photos
/2017/09/pumpkin-fairy-house.description: Carve a pumpkin fairy house step by step: draw the door and windows, cut them out, add steps and carved details, then light it up. Tips, tools and FAQ.
/2017/09/pumpkin-fairy-house.prepend: Quick answer: to carve a pumpkin fairy house, hollow out a pumpkin through a large lid (the lid becomes the roof), draw a round door and two windows with a washable marker, cut the windows right through, cut the door out in one piece and prop it below the opening as steps, then add carved or drawn details around the door and light it from inside.
/2017/09/pumpkin-fairy-house.append:
Pumpkin Fairy House Carving Tips

Updated October 2026: carving tips, design ideas and FAQ added by the Just Halloween Crafts team.

  • Cut through or score? Cut right through the flesh for windows and the doorway so light shines out. For brickwork, vines and the door frame, only peel away the orange skin to the pale layer underneath. Scored areas glow softly when the pumpkin is lit and are much easier than fine cut-outs.
  • Use the right tools: a small serrated pumpkin saw cuts curves more safely than a kitchen knife, and a clay loop tool or a lino cutter is ideal for scoring thin lines.
  • Work from the center out: cut the door and windows first, then the small details, so you're not pressing on fragile areas you've already carved.
  • Pick a tall pumpkin: a pumpkin that is taller than it is wide looks more like a cottage and leaves room for a door with windows on either side.

Pumpkin carving is a job for an adult or an older child with supervision. Younger children can draw the design and decorate the finished house with glitter glue, pins or stickers.

Drawing Your Fairy House Design

Draw the whole design on the pumpkin before you cut anything, using a washable marker so mistakes wipe off. Start with the door at the bottom center, then add the windows level with the top of the door, then the decoration. Good details to draw include:

  • A stone path or stepping stones running down from the door
  • Bricks or stones around the door frame
  • Climbing vines and leaves around the windows
  • Shutters, a tiny chimney near the stem, or a round attic window above the door

If you'd rather not carve at all, draw the same design with a black paint pen, or see our no-carve pumpkin decorating ideas.

Make Your Fairy House Last

Carved pumpkins soften and mold within days, so carve your fairy house no more than a few days before you want to show it off. Our guide on how to make a carved pumpkin last longer explains cleaning, sealing the cut edges and storage. Light it with battery LED candles or fairy lights: they're safer than a flame and don't cook the pumpkin from the inside. If you need help with the first step, see our tutorial on how to hollow out a pumpkin.

Pumpkin Fairy House FAQ

What tools do you need to carve a pumpkin fairy house?

You need a large spoon or scoop to hollow the pumpkin, a washable marker for the design, a small serrated pumpkin saw or a small sharp knife for cutting through, and a loop tool or lino cutter for scoring details. Toothpicks hold the door in place as steps.

How do you make the fairy house door?

Cut the door out in one whole piece, score lines across it to look like steps, then push half toothpicks into the bottom of the doorway and press the door piece onto them so it leans out like a little staircase.

Can kids make a pumpkin fairy house?

Children can draw the design and decorate the house with glitter glue, sequins, push pins or stickers, while an adult does the cutting. For a no-knife version, paint or draw the door and windows instead of carving them.

/2015/04/sugar-skull-perler-beads-patter.title: Sugar Skull Perler Bead Pattern: Easy Step-by-Step Guide
/2015/04/sugar-skull-perler-beads-patter.description: Make a sugar skull Perler bead pattern on a small square pegboard: black outline, white highlights, then 4 to 5 bright colors. Color ideas and ironing tips.
/2015/04/sugar-skull-perler-beads-patter.prepend: Quick answer: to make a sugar skull Perler bead pattern, lay the skull outline, eye sockets, nose and teeth in black on a small square pegboard, pick out a few white highlights, then fill the eye area and the rest of the skull with four or five bright colors. Cover with ironing paper and have an adult iron it to fuse the beads.
/2015/04/sugar-skull-perler-beads-patter.append:
Sugar Skull Color Ideas

Updated October 2026: color ideas, ironing tips and FAQ added by the Just Halloween Crafts team.

Keep the black outline and white highlights from the steps above, then choose four or five fill colors. More than that tends to look busy on a small board. Some combinations to try:

  • Bright and festive: pink, yellow, turquoise and orange
  • Halloween: orange, purple and lime green
  • Cool tones: two blues, lilac and white
  • Glow in the dark: swap the white highlights for glow beads so the face shows up when the lights are off
  • Reversed: a white outline on a black or dark purple skull

Ironing Tips for Fused Bead Skulls

Place ironing paper over the beads and iron with slow, circular movements on a medium setting until the beads just begin to merge. Let the design cool, lift it off the pegboard, flip it and iron the back lightly so it's strong enough to hang. Press it under a heavy book while it cools to stop it curling. Ironing is a job for an adult. Fuse beads are small parts, so keep them away from children under three.

About Sugar Skulls

Sugar skulls, or calaveras de azúcar, are part of the Day of the Dead (Día de los Muertos), celebrated in Mexico and by many families elsewhere on November 1 and 2 to remember loved ones who have died. Decorated skulls are placed on home altars, often with the person's name. Because they honor family members, sugar skull designs work best as cheerful, colorful decorations rather than as scary ones.

For more patterns, see our Halloween Perler bead patterns, the Perler bead spider web and the witch owl Perler pattern.

Sugar Skull Perler Bead FAQ

What size pegboard do I need for a sugar skull?

This pattern fits a small square pegboard, the kind that comes with many bead kits. On a large square board you can make a bigger, more detailed skull with extra rings of color around the eyes and flowers on the forehead.

How many colors should a Perler sugar skull have?

Use black for the outline, white for highlights, and four or five fill colors. On a small board, more colors than that start to look like random speckles instead of a deliberate pattern.

What can I make with a Perler sugar skull?

Fused skulls make good hanging decorations, fridge magnets, keychains and coasters. Glue a small magnet to the back, or thread fishing line or ribbon through an outer bead to hang it.

/2016/05/halloween-foam-craft-kits-kids.title: Halloween Foam Craft Kits for Kids: Ideas and Buying Tips
/2016/05/halloween-foam-craft-kits-kids.description: Halloween foam craft kits for kids: monster magnets, pumpkin sticker sets and a foam haunted house, plus what to look for in a kit and how to make your own.
/2016/05/halloween-foam-craft-kits-kids.prepend: Quick answer: Halloween foam craft kits are boxed sets of pre-cut, often self-adhesive foam shapes that children stick together to make monsters, masks, pumpkin faces or 3D decorations. Choose a kit by the age on the box, how many projects it makes and whether the pieces are self-adhesive, or make your own from foam sheets using the ideas on this page.
/2016/05/halloween-foam-craft-kits-kids.append:
What to Look for in a Halloween Foam Craft Kit

Updated October 2026: buying tips, a DIY kit idea and answers to common questions, added by the Just Halloween Crafts team.

The best kit is the one that matches the children who will use it. A few checks before you buy save a lot of frustration on the day.

  • The age label. Foam pieces, wiggly eyes and pom-poms are small, so follow the age shown on the box, and supervise younger children closely.
  • Self-adhesive or glue. Peel-and-stick pieces are quicker and less messy, which suits younger children and parties. Kits that need glue give older children more freedom to design their own monsters.
  • Number of projects. For a class or a party, a multi-pack where every child makes the same item is easier to run than one large model.
  • Finished size and use. Magnets, masks and door hangers are used afterwards; a 3D haunted house is a longer project better suited to older children or a family afternoon.

How to Make Your Own Halloween Foam Craft Kit

You can put together a homemade kit with a pack of craft foam sheets, a few templates and some extras. Cut out simple shapes in advance (bats, pumpkins, ghosts, tombstones, monster eyes and mouths), then pack each set in a zip bag with wiggly eyes, glue dots and a pipe cleaner or two.

  1. Print templates from our free printable Halloween crafts collection and trace them onto foam with a ballpoint pen.
  2. Cut the shapes with sharp scissors; adults can use a craft knife for small inside details.
  3. Bag one set per child with a picture of the finished idea so they know what to aim for.
  4. Add a magnet strip, a lolly stick or an elastic band so the finished piece becomes a fridge magnet, a puppet or a mask.
Tip: Foam masks are a natural next step. Our paper plate Halloween masks use the same cut-and-stick approach, and foam pieces stick to them well with glue dots.

What age are Halloween foam craft kits for?

Most foam kits are aimed at children of school age, but the right age depends on the kit, so check the label on the box. Peel-and-stick kits with large pieces are easiest for younger children; kits with lots of small parts or 3D assembly suit older children, ideally with an adult nearby.

What glue works best on craft foam?

Glue dots and double-sided foam tape work instantly and are clean for children to use. Tacky craft glue also holds well but needs drying time, so lay pieces flat while it sets. A low-temperature glue gun is strong too, but should be handled by an adult because the glue gets hot.

Are foam craft kits good for a Halloween party?

Yes. They need no paint, little setup and are easy to tidy away, which makes them a good choice for a party craft table. Give each child the same small project, such as a magnet or a mask, and keep it short for younger children so everyone finishes before attention runs out.

Planning a group activity? See our tips for a Halloween craft party for kids, more Halloween craft kits for kids, felt finger puppets and no-carve pumpkin decorating ideas, or browse all our crafts for kids.

/2015/07/how-to-make-maleficent-horn-hea.title: Maleficent Horns Headband DIY (Free Horn Template)
/2015/07/how-to-make-maleficent-horn-hea.description: Make a Maleficent horns headband from black card or craft foam: print the free horn template, trace it, cut it and fix the horns to a plain headband.
/2015/07/how-to-make-maleficent-horn-hea.prepend: Quick answer: to make a Maleficent horns headband, print the free horn template, trace it onto thick black card or craft foam with the headband laid along the bottom edge, cut the horns out, then fix them to a plain black headband with hot glue, tape or cord tied through punched holes.
/2015/07/how-to-make-maleficent-horn-hea.append:
Maleficent Horns Headband Tips

Updated October 2026: quick answer, extra tips and common questions added by the Just Halloween Crafts team.

Craft foam gives the lightest, most comfortable horns for children, while thick card holds a sharper curve and is easier to cut cleanly. Whichever you use, keep about an inch of solid material in the middle above the headband, because that strip carries the weight of both horns.

  • Floppy horns: glue a second layer of card or foam to the back, or slide a strip of thin cardboard between two foam layers.
  • Showing edges: run a black marker along the cut edges of light-cored card so they disappear against dark hair.
  • Headband slipping: choose a headband with small teeth, or wrap it in a strip of black felt so it grips the hair.
  • Want rounder horns? See the easy Maleficent headpiece, which builds the horns in a different way.

What can I use to make Maleficent horns?

Thick black card, craft foam or a sheet of sturdy plastic all work for flat horns on a headband. Card is cheapest and holds its shape, foam is lighter and softer for children, and plastic lasts longest. You also need a plain black headband, scissors and glue, tape or cord to attach the horns.

How do you attach horns to a headband?

The quickest way is a thin line of hot glue along the back of the horns, pressed onto the headband by an adult. Tape works but can catch in hair. For a glue-free option, punch three holes along the bottom of the horns and tie them to the headband with black elastic cord or twine.

Can kids make this headband?

Yes. Children can trace and cut card or foam horns with ordinary scissors, and the cord method needs no glue gun. An adult should handle any hot glue and check that the horns sit comfortably before the costume is worn for a whole evening.

Finish the look with a dark cloak from our guide to making a cloak without sewing, or make a matching Maleficent Perler bead pattern and Rainbow Loom bracelet. For more character headwear, try our homemade witch hat or browse the costume accessories section.
